case.label: C
case.text: Network Firewall stateful rules (Suricata-compatible) can inspect HTTP payloads, so a candidate could argue it blocks SQL injection; but the option names a domain list rule group, which matches domain names only, and the NAT gateway detail is a lure. Cue: 'does not write its own detection rules' points straight at managed rule groups. Not a defensible second answer.

case.label: B
case.text: Shield Advanced with the Shield Response Team would also stop the flood and the SRT can write WAF rules, but the monthly subscription fails MOST cost-effective and waiting for SRT per attack fails 'as soon as possible'. A fails because the ALB sees CloudFront addresses, not client addresses; C fails because security groups have no deny rules.

case.label: A
case.text: A scope-down rate-based rule on the sign-in path is cheap and quick, but with a few requests per address per hour from thousands of addresses an aggregate limit would block real users too, which the stem forbids. C is manual daily work and reacts a day late. No second answer survives the 'real users must keep signing in' constraint.

case.label: C
case.text: WAF with a rate-based rule is a common pick for 'attacks against the website', but it needs a new web ACL and works at layer 7, not against SYN floods or UDP reflection. Wording cue: B is the only option without an 'after ...' clause and says 'already active', which mirrors 'without a new subscription or new configuration' almost word for word; consider neutral phrasing such as 'AWS Shield Standard' alone.

case.label: B
case.text: B is less work up front and still gets SRT access and Shield Advanced protection once added; a candidate could argue it meets LEAST operational overhead because A adds rate-based rules the stem never asks for. It fails only if the reader knows that cost protection and SRT help depend on the resources already being protected (and prepared) before the attack; the stem leaves that to knowledge, which is fair. D adds Network Firewall that does nothing for a CloudFront/ALB layer-7 attack.

case.label: A
case.text: A names Firewall Manager, the right service, which tempts a fast reader; but Firewall Manager is set up once through an administrator account, not per account, and its WAF policies are per Region, so 'one policy that covers all Regions' is wrong. Slight tension: the stem says 'one set of AWS WAF rules' while D creates several policies; the same rule set in each policy still satisfies it.

case.label: B
case.text: A candidate who links the web ACL to the origin's Region would pick US West (Oregon), and the ALB there could take a regional web ACL; but the requirement is to protect the distribution, and CloudFront web ACLs and their IP sets must be created with global scope in US East (N. Virginia). The stem states the target clearly.

case.label: E
case.text: Putting endpoints in the workload subnets saves subnets and still has one endpoint per zone, so a candidate could call it equally resilient; but Network Firewall cannot inspect traffic that stays inside the subnet of its own endpoint, and AWS guidance is a dedicated firewall subnet per zone. A is a single point of failure; C fails because WAF does not attach to an internet gateway.

answers.flag: Option B says 'that web ACL', a reference with no antecedent in the stem or in B itself; it only makes sense when read with D, so it gives away the B+D pair (and reads as broken in a permuted order); rewrite B to name the web ACL on the distribution.

case.label: C
case.text: Shield Advanced adds automatic application layer DDoS mitigation for CloudFront and ALB, which directly targets an HTTP GET flood, so C is a technically valid protection; it fails only on MOST cost-effective because of the subscription fee. A also fails because the ALB subnets see CloudFront addresses, not client addresses. Main problem is the dangling 'that web ACL' cue in B.

case.label: D
case.text: A Lambda function in each account would detect and delete the rules, so it meets the functional need; but it is per-account code to deploy into every new account, which fails LEAST operational overhead and 'from a single location'. B blocks traffic but does not audit or fix the rules; A fails because WAF does not attach to EC2 instances or filter by port.

case.label: C
case.text: An open source WAF on each instance keeps the Network Load Balancer and does block SQL injection and XSS, so a candidate who sees 'move the traffic' as heavy migration work could pick it; but per-instance installs and weekly rule updates are more ongoing overhead than one managed web ACL. D is the trap: AWS WAF does not associate with a Network Load Balancer.

case.label: A
case.text: A self-managed proxy fleet can enforce an outbound domain allow list, so it meets the function; it fails LEAST operational overhead. D fails because WAF on the ALB inspects inbound web requests, not instance egress; C fails because security groups and network ACLs match IP addresses and ports, not domain names.
